newsitem.title: UK: World leaders applaud landmark NATO-Russia accord.
newsitem.headline: World leaders applaud landmark NATO-Russia accord.

text.p: World leaders on Wednesday applauded a landmark agreement reached between NATO and Russia mapping out a new relationship into the next century.

But eastern European countries hoping to be invited to start negotiations on entry to the Western defence alliance in July said the pact should not directly affect the timing or the terms of their membership.
In Moscow, Russian hardliners predictably attacked the agreement, while liberal politicians took a cautious line, awaiting more details.

"(The West) has often cheated Russia and they will probably cheat us this time as well as we have nothing to trade with," Albert Makashov, a communist deputy in the State Duma lower house of parliament, told reporters.
A spokesman for the White House said the United States was "very encouraged" at the breakthrough pact, aimed at sweeping away Moscow's concerns over NATO's expansion eastwards.
Germany also hailed the agreement, the result of months of tough negotiations between Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana.

Germany's Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, who has played a significant role in diplomatic efforts to make NATO's expansion plans more palatable to Russia, called the agreement "good news", and said he hoped it would lead to closer cooperation between Russia and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
"Russia must be fully involved in Europe's new security architecture," he said in a statement.
"We do not want any (security) troughs in Europe. I hope that the result of these talks will help to open the door to closer security cooperation with Russia."

Poland, expected to be among the first invitees for a new wave of entry to NATO, said the deal removed one of the important elements of dispute, but added that expansion would have gone ahead without it.

"Although the calender of NATO expansion would have been implemented regardless of the agreement, it will now proceed in a better climate, a better atmosphere," Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati told reporters.
He added: "The agreement should not create a second-class membership category and must in no way provide for delaying the alliance's expansion."
Hungary and the Czech Republic, are also expected to receive invitations to join the 16-member alliance at a NATO expansion summit in July, due to be hosted by Spain.
Hungarian Foreign Minister Laszlo Kovacs said he was sure NATO had not made concessions affecting potential new members in its agreement with Russia.
"We dont know the text of the agreement...but I have no reason to believe NATO has given any concession which would create diffulties for the countries which want to join NATO," Kovacs told Reuters.
Spain endorsed the historic accord, saying it was needed to reassure Moscow and facilitate "necessary expansion" of the western alliance to incorporate former Eastern bloc nations.
"This is very good news...(The accord) paves the way for this necessary expansion toward the democracies of central Europe," Spain's Foreign Minister Abel Matutes told a news conference.
Matutes said it was important that Russia felt secure and felt it had nothing to fear from its western flank.

Russia had been concerned about its former Warsaw Pact countries joining the alliance and has opposed moving NATO military infrastructure closer to its borders, saying that would pose a threat to national security.
A NATO-Russia joint statement on Wednesday said they had made "decisive progress" on key issues including military problems, which had been the main obstacles to agreement.
Romania and Slovenia also hope to be in the first wave of new entrants to come out of the July summit.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, who is due to discuss NATO-Russian relations during talks with his counterpart Yevgeny Primakov in Moscow next week, expressed "warm satisfaction" at the deal.

Dini described the partnership between NATO and Russia as an "important and historical objective" and said Italy hoped it would lead to "the establishment of a new and more secure architecture of peace and security in Europe".
Solana and Primakov said their agreement, which has secured a place in history for the 54-year-old Secretary-General, opened the way for the security deal to be signed in Paris on May 27.
